questions.text: In corporate finance and equity markets, what is the fundamental difference between a 'Rights Issue' and a 'Bonus Issue' of shares?

options.text: A rights issue is entirely free of cost to existing shareholders, whereas a bonus issue requires partial cash payments.
A rights issue dilutes the existing equity share capital of the firm, whereas a bonus issue keeps the total share volume identical.
A rights issue requires the existing shareholder to pay a specified subscription price to purchase additional shares, whereas a bonus issue allocates extra shares completely free of cost.
A rights issue is offered to external retail institutional buyers, whereas a bonus issue is reserved strictly for the company’s board of directors.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A rights issue requires the existing shareholder to pay a specified subscription price to purchase additional shares, whereas a bonus issue allocates extra shares completely free of cost.

Key Points

  • A Rights Issue is an invitation to existing shareholders to purchase additional new shares of the company at a discounted price (lower than the current market price) within a specific period. It is a method used by companies to raise fresh equity capital from the existing investor base. Hence, the statement regarding the subscription price in Option C is correct.
  • A Bonus Issue, also known as a scrip issue or capitalization issue, refers to the distribution of additional shares to existing shareholders without any additional cost. These shares are issued in proportion to the shares already held by the investor. Hence, the statement regarding bonus issues being free of cost in Option C is correct.
  • In a Rights Issue, the company receives cash inflow from shareholders who choose to exercise their rights to buy shares. In contrast, a Bonus Issue involves no cash flow; it is essentially an accounting entry where the company transfers funds from its accumulated reserves (like General Reserve or Securities Premium Account) to its share capital.
  • Both corporate actions result in an increase in the total number of outstanding shares of the company. Consequently, the Earnings Per Share (EPS) and the market price per share usually adjust downward to reflect the increased supply of shares in the equity market.
  • Option A is incorrect because a Rights Issue is not free; shareholders must pay a subscription price. Option B is incorrect because both issues increase the total share volume, not just the rights issue. Option D is incorrect because both are primarily offered to existing shareholders, not external institutional buyers or strictly the board of directors.

Additional Information

  • Regulatory Framework in India: In India, the issuance of rights and bonus shares is governed by the Companies Act, 2013. Specifically, Section 62 deals with the further issue of share capital (Rights Issue), while Section 63 deals with the issue of bonus shares. Furthermore, listed companies must comply with the SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, 2018.
  • Renunciation of Rights: One unique feature of a Rights Issue is that the "rights" are often renounceable. This means if an existing shareholder does not wish to buy more shares, they can sell their Rights Entitlements (REs) to other investors on the stock exchange platform during the rights trading window. Bonus shares cannot be "renounced" in this manner as they are automatically credited to eligible holders.
  • Capitalization of Reserves: A Bonus Issue is a sign of a company’s financial health and confidence, as it indicates that the company has sufficient reserves to convert into share capital. According to Section 63, bonus shares can be issued out of Free Reserves, Securities Premium Account, or Capital Redemption Reserve account, but cannot be issued by revaluation of fixed assets.
  • Objective of the Issues: Companies typically announce a Rights Issue when they need capital for expansion, debt reduction, or acquisitions. On the other hand, the primary objective of a Bonus Issue is to increase the liquidity of the stock by making it more affordable for retail investors and to reward shareholders without depleting cash reserves.

Important Points

  • Record Date: For both actions, the company announces a Record Date. Only those shareholders whose names appear in the Register of Members or Depository records on this specific date are eligible to receive the bonus shares or the right to subscribe to new shares.
  • Proportion/Ratio: Both issues are expressed in ratios. For example, a 1:5 Bonus Issue means an investor gets 1 share free for every 5 shares held. Similarly, a 2:7 Rights Issue means the investor can buy 2 new shares for every 7 shares they currently own.
  • Impact on Net Worth: A Rights Issue increases the Net Worth of the company because new capital is introduced. A Bonus Issue does not change the total Net Worth; it only reshuffles the internal components of Shareholders' Equity.
  • Taxation: In the context of Income Tax in India, the cost of acquisition for Bonus Shares is considered Zero for the purpose of calculating Capital Gains Tax. For Rights Shares, the cost of acquisition is the actual subscription price paid to the company.

questions.text: When the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) conducts an 'Open Market Operation' (OMO) involving the outright sale of government securities in the secondary market, what is the primary intended macroeconomic outcome?

options.text: To inject liquid cash into the banking system to lower inter-bank lending rates.
To absorb excess liquidity from the banking system and exert upward pressure on short-term interest rates.
To directly finance the fiscal deficit of the central government for the ongoing quarter.
To devalue the Indian Rupee against major global currencies to aggressively boost export performance.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is To absorb excess liquidity from the banking system and exert upward pressure on short-term interest rates.

Key Points

  • Open Market Operations (OMO) refer to the buying and selling of government securities (G-Secs) by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) in the secondary market to regulate the money supply and liquidity conditions in the economy.
  • When the RBI conducts an outright sale of government securities, it receives payments from commercial banks and financial institutions, which results in the absorption of excess liquidity from the banking system. Hence, statement B is correct.
  • The reduction in the liquidity or cash reserves available with banks decreases their capacity to lend, which tends to exert upward pressure on short-term interest rates, such as the call money rate.
  • By selling securities, the RBI aims to reduce the money supply in the system to curb inflationary pressures and maintain macroeconomic stability.
  • Conversely, injecting liquid cash (Option A) is achieved through the purchase of securities, not their sale. Hence, statement A is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Monetary Policy Tool: OMO is one of the quantitative instruments of monetary policy used by the RBI to adjust the Rupee liquidity on a durable basis. It is distinct from the Liquidity Adjustment Facility (LAF), which manages short-term day-to-day liquidity.
  • Government Securities (G-Secs): These are tradable instruments issued by the Central Government or State Governments. They are considered sovereign debt and are often referred to as gilt-edged securities because they carry practically zero risk of default.
  • Impact on Yields: An outright sale of securities increases the supply of bonds in the market. As the supply increases, the market price of these securities typically falls, which causes the bond yields to increase.
  • Inflation Control: During periods of high inflation, the RBI may resort to selling securities to suck out liquidity, thereby making credit more expensive and slowing down aggregate demand in the economy.
  • Sterilization: This is a process where the RBI uses OMOs to neutralize the effect of foreign exchange inflows. If the RBI buys dollars to prevent the Rupee from appreciating, it injects Rupee liquidity, which it then mops up by selling G-Secs through OMO.

Important Points

  • Fiscal Deficit Financing: While OMOs involve government securities, their primary purpose is monetary management and not the direct financing of the fiscal deficit. Direct financing of the government's deficit by the central bank is generally restricted to maintain fiscal discipline. Hence, statement C is incorrect.
  • Exchange Rate Management: Although changes in interest rates resulting from OMOs can influence the exchange rate, the primary intended macroeconomic outcome of a domestic OMO sale is liquidity management, not the aggressive devaluation of the Indian Rupee to boost exports. Hence, statement D is incorrect.
  • Types of OMOs: There are two types: Outright Purchase/Sale, which is permanent, and Repo/Reverse Repo transactions under the LAF, which are temporary and involve a repurchase agreement.
  • RBI Act, 1934: The legal authority for the RBI to conduct Open Market Operations is derived from the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934, allowing it to maintain price stability while supporting economic growth.
  • Secondary Market: OMOs are conducted in the secondary market, typically through the Negotiated Dealing System-Order Matching (NDS-OM) platform, where commercial banks, primary dealers, and insurance companies participate.

questions.text: Under the provisions of the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), what does the term 'Capital Account Transaction' refer to?

options.text: A transaction that alters the foreign assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of a person resident in India.
A transaction undertaken specifically to settle day-to-day short-term international trade payments or interest on loans.
A transaction involving personal remittances sent by non-resident family members to meet living expenses in India.
A short-term overdraft facility extended by an Indian bank branch to an overseas corporate importer.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A transaction that alters the foreign assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of a person resident in India..

Key Points

  • According to Section 2(e) of the Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999, a Capital Account Transaction is defined as a transaction that alters the assets or liabilities, including contingent liabilities, outside India of persons resident in India. It also includes transactions that alter assets or liabilities in India of persons resident outside India. Hence, option A is correct.
  • The primary distinction between a capital account and a current account transaction lies in whether the transaction creates a future claim or liability. A Capital Account Transaction specifically involves investment flows and loans that change the financial status or balance sheet of a resident or non-resident.
  • A transaction undertaken specifically to settle day-to-day short-term international trade payments or interest on loans is categorized as a Current Account Transaction under Section 2(j) of the act. These are revenue-nature transactions rather than capital-nature. Hence, option B is incorrect.
  • Transactions involving personal remittances sent by non-resident family members to meet living expenses in India are also classified as Current Account Transactions. These are considered unrequited transfers for consumption rather than asset creation. Hence, option C is incorrect.
  • A short-term overdraft facility or banking credit extended in the ordinary course of international trade (such as Letters of Credit or Trade Credit) is generally treated as a Current Account Transaction to facilitate commerce. Hence, option D is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • The Foreign Exchange Management Act (FEMA), 1999:
    • This act was enacted by the Parliament of India to replace the more stringent Foreign Exchange Regulation Act (FERA) of 1973.
    • It came into force on June 1, 2000, with the objective of facilitating external trade and payments and promoting the orderly development and maintenance of the foreign exchange market in India.
    • Unlike FERA, which was based on prohibition, FEMA is based on management and regulation.
  • Current Account Transactions (Section 2(j)):
    • These are transactions other than capital account transactions. They include payments due in connection with foreign trade, other current business, services, and short-term banking and credit facilities.
    • It also includes interest on loans and net income from investments, as well as remittances for family maintenance, medical expenses, and foreign travel/education.
  • Permissible Capital Account Transactions:
    • Section 6 of FEMA empowers the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) to specify, in consultation with the Central Government, any class or classes of Capital Account Transactions which are permissible.
    • Examples include Investment in foreign securities, Acquisition of immovable property outside India, Foreign Currency Loans (ECBs), and Transfer of residency.
  • Regulatory Authority:
    • The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) is the chief controller of foreign exchange. While Current Account Transactions are generally free (subject to certain reasonable restrictions), Capital Account Transactions are regulated.
    • The Enforcement Directorate (ED) is responsible for investigating contraventions of the provisions of FEMA.

Important Points

  • Residential Status: Under FEMA, a Person Resident in India is defined based on the number of days spent in the country. Generally, an individual must reside in India for more than 182 days during the preceding financial year to be considered a resident, though this is subject to the purpose of their stay (e.g., employment, business).
  • Contingent Liabilities: These refer to potential liabilities that may occur depending on the outcome of an uncertain future event, such as guarantees given by a resident to a person residing outside India. These are explicitly included in the definition of Capital Account Transactions.
  • Liberalized Remittance Scheme (LRS): This is a policy under FEMA that allows resident individuals to freely remit up to USD 250,000 per financial year for any permissible current or capital account transaction or a combination of both.

questions.text: In the context of the money market, what is the core operational distinction between a Call Money, Notice Money, and Term Money transaction?

options.text: Call Money involves borrowing for up to 24 hours, Notice Money ranges from 2 to 14 days, and Term Money exceeds 14 days.
Call Money is exclusively handled by corporate firms, while Notice and Term Money are strictly limited to the Reserve Bank of India.
Call Money requires 100% collateral in the form of Treasury Bills, whereas Notice and Term Money are completely unsecured.
Call Money is used to meet the Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR), while Notice and Term Money fulfill the Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR).
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Call Money involves borrowing for up to 24 hours, Notice Money ranges from 2 to 14 days, and Term Money exceeds 14 days.

Key Points

  • Call Money is a vital component of the inter-bank money market where funds are borrowed or lent for a very short duration, specifically for one day or overnight (up to 24 hours). It allows banks to manage their immediate liquidity requirements and meet temporary mismatches in cash flows. Hence, the definition of Call Money in the option is correct.
  • Notice Money refers to the borrowing and lending of funds for a period spanning between 2 days and 14 days. In this arrangement, the lender or the borrower can call for or return the money with a short notice. This instrument is essential for banks to adjust their liquidity positions over a slightly longer horizon than overnight. Hence, the definition of Notice Money in the option is correct.
  • Term Money involves the borrowing and lending of funds for a duration exceeding 14 days. This market helps financial institutions and banks secure funds for longer durations, usually up to 90 days or as per Reserve Bank of India (RBI) guidelines, to meet specific structural liquidity needs. Hence, the definition of Term Money in the option is correct.
  • These three instruments—Call, Notice, and Term Money—are predominantly used by Scheduled Commercial Banks and Primary Dealers to maintain the required Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR) and Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR) levels.
  • The interest rates in these markets, such as the Mumbai Inter-Bank Offer Rate (MIBOR), are market-driven and reflect the liquidity conditions in the banking system.

Additional Information

  • Participants in the Market: The Call, Notice, and Term Money markets in India are restricted to specific entities to ensure stability. The primary participants include Scheduled Commercial Banks (excluding Regional Rural Banks), Co-operative Banks (other than Land Development Banks), and Primary Dealers (PDs). Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs) and Corporates are generally not permitted to participate as lenders or borrowers in this specific inter-bank market segment.
  • Unsecured Nature: One of the defining features of these transactions is that they are unsecured. This means no collateral (like Government Securities or Treasury Bills) is required to back the transaction. The lending is based entirely on the creditworthiness of the borrowing institution.
  • Prudential Limits: To prevent excessive volatility and manage systemic risk, the Reserve Bank of India prescribes prudential limits on the amount that banks and Primary Dealers can borrow and lend in the Call/Notice/Term Money market. For Scheduled Commercial Banks, the internal limit is often tied to their Capital Funds or Net Owned Funds.
  • Market Volatility: The interest rates in the Call Money Market are known for their high volatility. Rates can spike significantly during periods of tight liquidity, such as reporting Fridays (when banks must report their CRR positions) or during advance tax payment periods.

Important Points

  • Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR): This is the percentage of Net Demand and Time Liabilities (NDTL) that banks are required to keep with the RBI in cash. Shortfalls in CRR are a primary driver for banks to enter the Call Money market.
  • Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR): This is the portion of NDTL that banks must maintain in the form of liquid assets like Gold, Cash, or unencumbered Government Securities. While Call Money primarily helps with cash, it indirectly supports SLR management by freeing up funds.
  • Regulatory Framework: The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), under the RBI Act, 1934, regulates the money market. It issues Master Directions periodically to update the eligibility, limits, and reporting requirements for all money market instruments.
  • Reporting Mechanism: All transactions in this market must be reported on the Negotiated Dealing System-Call (NDS-CALL) platform within 15 minutes of the trade to ensure transparency and real-time monitoring by the regulator.

questions.text: In the Indian capital markets, Participatory Notes (P-Notes or PNs) are frequently a subject of regulatory scrutiny by SEBI. Which of the following statements accurately describes a Participatory Note?

options.text: They are debt instruments issued by the Government of India to overseas citizen investors to fund infrastructure projects.
They are derivative instruments issued by registered Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) to overseas investors who wish to invest in Indian equities without registering directly with SEBI.
They are specialized instruments issued by commercial banks to corporate houses to settle cross-border import liabilities.
They are equity shares with differential voting rights offered exclusively to institutional venture capitalists.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is They are derivative instruments issued by registered Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) to overseas investors who wish to invest in Indian equities without registering directly with SEBI.

Key Points

  • Participatory Notes (P-Notes), also referred to as Offshore Derivative Instruments (ODIs), are financial instruments used by foreign investors to invest in Indian securities such as shares, bonds, and derivatives.
  • These instruments are issued by registered Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) to overseas investors who want to gain exposure to the Indian capital market without having to register themselves directly with the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI). Hence, statement B is correct.
  • The FPI acts as an intermediary; it purchases the securities on the Indian stock exchanges (like NSE or BSE) and then issues P-Notes to the offshore client, passing on the dividends and capital gains generated from the underlying assets.
  • P-Notes are not debt instruments issued by the government for infrastructure; they are private contracts between FPIs and their clients. Hence, statement A is incorrect.
  • They are not banking instruments for import liabilities, nor are they equity shares with differential voting rights for venture capitalists. Hence, statements C and D are incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Anonymity and Regulation: Historically, P-Notes were popular because they allowed investors to remain anonymous. However, to curb money laundering and round-tripping (where untaxed money leaves the country and returns as foreign investment), SEBI has introduced stringent Know Your Customer (KYC) norms.
  • Reporting Requirements: Since 2017, SEBI has mandated that FPIs must report the ultimate beneficial owners of P-Notes on a monthly basis. This ensures that the regulator knows exactly who is pumping money into the Indian economy.
  • Taxation: In the Union Budget 2018, the government introduced a Long-Term Capital Gains (LTCG) tax of 10% on gains exceeding Rs. 1 lakh, which also applies to investments made through the P-Note route, bringing parity with direct FPI investments.
  • Market Significance: While P-Notes once accounted for nearly 50% of the total FPI investment in India (peaking around 2007), their share has significantly dropped to less than 5% of the total Assets Under Management (AUM) as registration for FPIs has become simpler and more transparent.

Important Points

  • Eligibility Criteria: According to SEBI (Foreign Portfolio Investors) Regulations, 2019, P-Notes can only be issued to entities that are regulated by an appropriate foreign regulatory body. This includes Sovereign Wealth Funds, Pension Funds, and Central Banks.
  • Impact on Liquidity: Despite the regulations, P-Notes remain an important tool for providing liquidity to Indian markets, especially from institutional investors who may not want to deal with the administrative overhead of maintaining a direct Demat account in India.
  • Anti-Money Laundering (AML): Issuers of P-Notes are required to comply with Anti-Money Laundering standards and must ensure that the P-Notes are not issued to Non-Resident Indians (NRIs) or Resident Indians.
  • Transferability: P-Notes can be transferred from one offshore investor to another, but only with the prior consent of the issuing FPI and provided the new investor also meets SEBI's eligibility and KYC criteria.

questions.text: An investor purchases a 'Put Option' on a specific banking stock traded on the exchange. Under what market condition will this investor maximize their potential financial gains?

options.text: When the market price of the underlying banking stock falls significantly below the option's strike price.
When the market price of the stock rises drastically above the option's strike price.
When the stock price remains completely stagnant and enters a tight consolidation phase.
When the issuing bank announces a higher-than-expected quarterly dividend payout.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is When the market price of the underlying banking stock falls significantly below the option's strike price.

Key Points

  • A Put Option is a financial derivative contract that grants the buyer the right, but not the legal obligation, to sell a specific quantity of an underlying asset at a predetermined strike price within a set timeframe.
  • Investors purchase put options when they hold a bearish outlook on a stock. The potential for financial gain is maximized when the market price of the underlying security crashes or falls significantly below the strike price. Hence, statement A is correct.
  • If the stock price increases drastically, the put option becomes "out-of-the-money." In this scenario, the investor would choose not to exercise the right to sell at a lower strike price, leading to a loss of the premium paid. Hence, statement B is incorrect.
  • In a stagnant market or consolidation phase, the value of the option erodes due to time decay (also known as Theta). As the expiration date approaches, the time value of the option reaches zero, which is detrimental to the buyer. Hence, statement C is incorrect.
  • While a dividend payout usually results in a minor downward adjustment of the stock price on the ex-dividend date, it is rarely sufficient to "maximize" gains unless it triggers a wider sell-off in the banking sector. Hence, statement D is incorrect.

Additional Information

  • Strike Price: This is the fixed price at which the put option holder can sell the stock. It is determined at the inception of the contract. If a banking stock has a strike price of 1000 and the market price drops to 700, the intrinsic value is 300.
  • Premium: This represents the market price of the option itself. It is the maximum risk for the buyer, while the potential profit for a put buyer is capped only by the stock price falling to zero.
  • Hedging Strategy: Put options are frequently used by institutional investors as insurance. For example, if an investor owns shares of a bank, they might buy a put option to protect against a market downturn or a financial crisis.
  • Option Greeks: Professional traders use Delta, Gamma, Vega, and Theta to measure the sensitivity of the option price to changes in the underlying stock price, volatility, and time.
  • In-the-Money (ITM): A put option is considered ITM when the current market price is lower than the strike price. This is the state where the option holds tangible value.

Important Points

  • Leverage: Options provide high leverage, meaning a small change in the stock price can result in a percentage gain that is many times higher than the actual price movement of the stock.
  • Break-even Calculation: For a put option buyer, the break-even point is reached when the market price equals the Strike Price minus the Premium. Profit only accrues when the stock falls below this numerical value.
  • Market Volatility: High implied volatility increases the Vega of the option, making the option more expensive. A sudden spike in market fear often benefits put holders as the demand for downside protection increases.
  • Exchange Regulation: In India, these products are regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and are traded on platforms like the National Stock Exchange (NSE).

questions.text: Which of the following bodies acts as the central counterparty and provides guaranteed clearing and settlement functions for transactions executed in government securities, money market instruments, and foreign exchange in India?

options.text: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)
National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL)
Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL)
Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC)
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL).

Key Points

  • The Clearing Corporation of India Limited (CCIL) was set up in April 2001 to provide guaranteed clearing and settlement functions for transactions in Government Securities, Money Market instruments, and Foreign Exchange.
  • It commenced its operations in February 2002 and acts as a Central Counterparty (CCP), which means it steps in between the buyer and seller to provide a settlement guarantee, thereby mitigating counterparty risk.
  • The CCIL was promoted by several major financial institutions and banks in India, including the State Bank of India (SBI), IDBI Bank, ICICI Bank, Life Insurance Corporation of India (LIC), Bank of Baroda, and HDFC Bank.
  • It is regulated by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) under the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007, and is designated as a Qualified Central Counterparty (QCCP).
  • By providing a centralized clearing and settlement mechanism, CCIL enhances efficiency, transparency, and liquidity in the Indian financial markets.

Additional Information

  • Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI):
    • SEBI was established on April 12, 1988, and given statutory powers on January 30, 1992, through the SEBI Act, 1992.
    • Its primary function is to protect the interests of investors in securities and to promote the development and regulation of the securities market in India.
    • It regulates stock exchanges, brokers, mutual funds, and portfolio managers.
  • National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL):
    • NSDL was the first electronic securities depository in India, established in August 1996.
    • It facilitates the holding of securities like shares, bonds, and debentures in dematerialized (electronic) form, making trading and transfer faster and safer.
  • Financial Stability and Development Council (FSDC):
    • The FSDC is a non-statutory apex council under the Ministry of Finance, constituted in December 2010.
    • It is chaired by the Union Finance Minister of India and focuses on financial stability, inter-regulatory coordination, and financial literacy.

Important Points

  • Segments of Operation: CCIL operates in various segments including the G-Sec Segment (Secondary market trades), Forex Segment (Inter-bank USD-INR), and Money Market Segment (Triparty Repo).
  • Forex Settlement: CCIL provides settlement for Inter-bank USD-INR spot, cash, and tom transactions on a Payment versus Payment (PvP) basis, which eliminates Herstatt risk.
  • Trade Repository: CCIL also acts as a Trade Repository for Over-the-Counter (OTC) interest rate and forex derivative transactions as mandated by the RBI.
  • Legal Entity Identifier (LEI): Through its subsidiary, Legal Entity Identifier India Limited (LEIL), CCIL acts as a local operating unit for issuing LEI codes, which are 20-digit unique numbers used to identify parties to financial transactions globally.

questions.text: Consider the functioning of the Indian derivatives market. What is the primary operational difference between a 'Forward Contract' and a 'Futures Contract'?

options.text: Forward contracts are highly regulated by SEBI, whereas futures contracts are completely unregulated.
Forward contracts are standardized and traded on recognized stock exchanges, while futures contracts are customized OTC contracts.
Futures contracts are standardized and cleared through an exchange clearinghouse, while forward contracts are customized over-the-counter (OTC) agreements.
Forward contracts require daily mark-to-market margin settlements, whereas futures contracts are settled only on the final expiry date.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is Futures contracts are standardized and cleared through an exchange clearinghouse, while forward contracts are customized over-the-counter (OTC) agreements.

Key Points

  • A Forward Contract is a private and customized agreement between two parties to buy or sell an underlying asset at a specific price on a future date. These contracts are traded Over-the-Counter (OTC) and not on a centralized exchange. Hence, statement B is incorrect as it swaps the definitions.
  • Futures Contracts are standardized agreements in terms of quantity, quality, and delivery date, which allows them to be traded on organized Stock Exchanges such as the National Stock Exchange (NSE) and Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE). Hence, statement C is correct.
  • The Clearinghouse of the exchange acts as a middleman for every Futures transaction, becoming the buyer to every seller and the seller to every buyer, which effectively eliminates counterparty risk or default risk. In contrast, Forward contracts rely entirely on the creditworthiness of the parties involved.
  • Forward contracts are generally unregulated as they are private bilateral agreements, while Futures contracts are strictly regulated by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) in the Indian context. Hence, statement A is incorrect.
  • In terms of settlement, Futures involve a daily mark-to-market (MTM) process where profits and losses are settled at the end of each trading day. Forward contracts are usually settled only at the maturity date of the contract. Hence, statement D is incorrect as it attributes daily settlement to forwards.

Additional Information

  • Derivatives Market in India: Trading in derivatives started in India in June 2000 following the recommendations of the L.C. Gupta Committee. The Securities Contracts (Regulation) Act, 1956 (SCRA) provides the legal framework for derivative trading, defining them as contracts that derive value from an underlying asset like stocks, indices, commodities, or currencies.
  • Standardization: In Futures, the exchange determines the lot size (e.g., 50 units for Nifty 50) and expiry dates (usually the last Thursday of the month), whereas Forwards allow parties to decide any amount and any date.
  • Margin Requirements: To trade in Futures, participants must maintain an Initial Margin and a Maintenance Margin with the broker. This ensures that the Clearing Corporation can cover potential losses from price fluctuations. Forwards typically do not require such formal margin structures, although collateral may be pledged.
  • Liquidity and Exit: Futures are highly liquid, allowing traders to "square off" or exit their positions at any time before expiry by taking an opposite position. Forward contracts are difficult to cancel or transfer because they are tailored to the specific needs of the two original parties, making them illiquid.
  • Physical vs. Cash Settlement: While many Futures in India (especially Equity Derivatives) are now physically settled as per SEBI mandates of 2018-2019, Forwards are frequently settled through the physical delivery of the asset, such as in Agricultural or Foreign Exchange transactions.

Important Points

  • Participants: The market consists of Hedgers (who want to reduce risk), Speculators (who take risks for profit), and Arbitrageurs (who profit from price differences in different markets).
  • Regulation: All exchange-traded derivatives (Futures and Options) are under the jurisdiction of SEBI, while OTC derivatives like Interest Rate Swaps (IRS) and Forward Rate Agreements (FRA) are primarily overseen by the Reserve Bank of India (RBI).
  • Major Indices: The most traded futures in India are based on the Nifty 50 and Bank Nifty indices on the NSE, which has consistently been ranked as one of the largest derivative exchanges in the world by trading volume according to the Futures Industry Association (FIA).

questions.text: In the Indian capital market, what does the term 'Greenshoe Option' signify during an Initial Public Offering (IPO)?

options.text: A clause that mandates the issuing company to invest 10% of the proceeds into eco-friendly or green initiatives.
A price-stabilizing mechanism that allows the underwriters to issue additional shares to the public in case of over-subscription.
A specialized tax exemption granted by SEBI to foreign portfolio investors investing in renewable energy stocks.
The automatic conversion of standard equity shares into differential voting rights (DVR) shares after listing.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is A price-stabilizing mechanism that allows the underwriters to issue additional shares to the public in case of over-subscription.

Key Points

  • The Greenshoe Option, technically known as an over-allotment option, is a provision in an underwriting agreement that grants the underwriter the right to sell more shares to investors than originally planned by the issuer. Hence, the statement in option B is correct.
  • In the Indian capital market, this mechanism is primarily used for price stabilization of a security immediately after its listing on the stock exchanges like NSE or BSE.
  • According to SEBI (Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements) Regulations, the maximum number of shares that can be over-allotted under this option is 15% of the total issue size.
  • The stabilizing agent (usually a merchant banker or underwriter) borrows shares from the promoters or pre-issue shareholders to allot them to the public in case of high demand during the Initial Public Offering (IPO).
  • If the stock price falls below the issue price after listing, the stabilizing agent buys shares back from the market using the funds collected from the over-allotment to support the price. Hence, the statement in option A is incorrect as it does not relate to eco-friendly initiatives.

Additional Information

  • Origin of the Term: The name comes from the Green Shoe Manufacturing Company (now known as Stride Rite Corporation), which was the first to use this mechanism in 1919 during its public offering.
  • Stabilization Period: Under SEBI guidelines, the stabilization process can be carried out for a maximum period of 30 days from the date when trading permission is granted by the stock exchange.
  • Regulatory Framework: The process is strictly governed by the Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) to prevent market manipulation. Any profit made by the stabilizing agent from buying shares at a lower price is transferred to the Investor Protection and Education Fund (IPEF).
  • Investor Protection: This option acts as a safety net for retail investors and institutional investors by mitigating the risk of a sharp decline in share prices immediately after the listing date.
  • Taxation and Exemptions: There is no specialized tax exemption granted specifically to Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) for using this option in renewable energy stocks. Hence, the statement in option C is incorrect.
  • Differential Voting Rights (DVR): The Greenshoe Option has no legal or functional connection to the conversion of equity into DVR shares. Hence, the statement in option D is incorrect.

Important Points

  • Full vs. Partial Greenshoe: A Full Greenshoe occurs when the underwriter exercises the option to buy the entire 15% of additional shares, whereas a Partial Greenshoe involves buying only a portion of those shares based on market conditions.
  • Over-subscription: This mechanism is typically triggered when an IPO is over-subscribed, meaning the demand for shares exceeds the supply offered by the company.
  • GSO Agreement: The company must disclose the Greenshoe Option (GSO) in its Draft Red Herring Prospectus (DRHP) and Red Herring Prospectus (RHP) to inform potential investors about the stabilization mechanism.
  • Escrow Account: The money received from the over-allotment of shares is kept in a separate GSO Bank Account (Escrow account) and is used exclusively for the purpose of market intervention.

questions.text: Commercial Paper (CP) is a widely used money market instrument in India. Which of the following conditions accurately reflects the operational guidelines stipulated by the Reserve Bank of India for issuing CPs?

options.text: CPs can be issued for a maturity period ranging anywhere from 30 days up to 3 years.
CPs must be issued only in denominations of ₹10,000 or multiples thereof.
Only manufacturing companies are permitted to issue CPs; financial institutions are strictly barred.
CPs are issued at a discount to the face value and are held in a dematerialized form.
None of the above

questions.explanation:
The correct answer is CPs are issued at a discount to the face value and are held in a dematerialized form.

Key Points

  • Commercial Paper (CP) is an unsecured money market instrument issued in the form of a promissory note. It was introduced in India in 1990 to enable highly rated corporate borrowers to diversify their sources of short-term borrowings.
  • Statement A is incorrect because CPs can be issued for maturities between a minimum of 7 days and a maximum of up to one year from the date of issue. They do not extend to 3 years as suggested. Hence, statement A is incorrect.
  • Statement B is incorrect because CPs are issued in denominations of ₹5 lakh and multiples thereof. The suggestion of ₹10,000 is inaccurate according to RBI guidelines. Hence, statement B is incorrect.
  • Statement C is incorrect because eligibility is not restricted to manufacturing companies. Corporates, primary dealers (PDs), and All-India Financial Institutions (FIs) are permitted to raise short-term resources through CPs. Hence, statement C is incorrect.
  • Statement D is correct because CPs are issued at a discount to face value as determined by the issuer. Furthermore, RBI mandates that CPs must be issued in dematerialized form through any of the depositories registered with SEBI. Hence, statement D is correct.

Additional Information

  • Eligibility Criteria: A corporate is eligible to issue CP provided its tangible net worth is not less than ₹4 crore, as per the latest audited balance sheet. Additionally, the working capital position should be sound, and the borrowal account must be classified as a Standard Asset by the financing banks.
  • Credit Rating Requirement: All eligible participants must obtain a credit rating for issuance of CP from agencies like CRISIL, ICRA, CARE, or FITCH. The minimum credit rating shall be 'A2' as per the rating symbol prescribed by SEBI.
  • Issuing and Paying Agent (IPA): Only a scheduled bank can act as an IPA for issuance of CP. The IPA verifies all documents and ensures the issuer has the authorized limit to raise funds.
  • Investment and Trading: CPs can be held by individuals, banking companies, other corporate bodies (registered or incorporated in India), and unincorporated bodies, Non-Resident Indians (NRIs), and Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) within the limits set by RBI.
  • Secondary Market: There is an active secondary market for CPs, and OTC (Over-the-Counter) trades must be reported on the FIMMDA (Fixed Income Money Market and Derivatives Association of India) reporting platform within 15 minutes of the trade.

Important Points

  • Regulatory Framework: The issuance of Commercial Paper is governed by the Reserve Bank of India under Section 45W of the RBI Act, 1934.
  • Buyback of CP: Issuers may buyback the CP, in full or part, before maturity. However, such buyback cannot take place before 30 days from the date of issue.
  • Purpose of Funds: CPs are typically used to meet working capital requirements or for "bridge financing" before a company secures long-term funding.
  • Underwriting: No issuer shall have the CP issue underwritten or co-accepted, ensuring it remains a market-driven unsecured instrument.
  • Default Reporting: In case of a default in repayment of a CP, the IPA must immediately report the details to the RBI through the standard reporting portal.
